451	
452	                                                               Discussion
453	
454	                                                               The results from this study suggest that players are 1.8 times more likely to tear their ACL during
455	
456	                                                               a long week compared to a normal week and 1.5 times more likely to tear their ACL during a
457	
458	                                                               short week compared to a normal week. No other factors, including games occurring before or
459	
460	                                                               after week 9, player demographics, playing surface type, or years of experience were
461	                                                                significantly associated with a higher risk of ACL tear during the NFL season. These findings
462	
463	                                                               highlight the need for the NFL Players Association and the NFL Competition Committee to
464	
465	                                                               consider the risk versus benefit of short and long breaks between games, as these may place
466	
467	                                                               players at an increased risk for ACL tear. While short weeks in the NFL season are used to
468	
469	                                                               increase the number of teams that play primetime games, allowing the NFL to maximize
470	
471	                                                               advertising revenue, the risk to the players’ health may not be worth the increased revenue. 26
472	
473	
474	
475	
476	This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
477	                                                               Previous studies have reported conflicting results on whether the duration of rest between games
478	
479	
480	
481	
482	                                                                                                                                                                                 Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
483	                                                               has an impact on the risk of ACL tears.21,22,27,28 Lawrence et al. used different determinates for
484	
485	                                                               short, normal, and long weeks, (4, 6-8, and 10-15 days respectively) and categorized injuries into
486	
487	
488	
489	
490	                                                                                                                                                                    Accepted Manuscript
491	                                                               knee, ankle, hamstring, shoulder, and concussion injuries for the 2012-2013 through 2013-2014
492	
493	                                                               seasons. Their study reported that across all injury types collected, there was no significant
494	
495	                                                               change in risk depending on the rest time between games.21 Perez et al. analyzed injuries that
496	
497	                                                               resulted in a loss of playing time during NFL seasons between 2013 and 2016 and found a
498	
499	                                                               decreased incidence during long and short weeks compared to normal weeks.22 This study also
500	
501	                                                               reports a decreased injury risk specifically for linebackers, fullbacks, and tight ends on a short
502	
503	                                                               week, which was not supported in the current study. Sharma et al. found that long weeks had a
504	
505	                                                               protective effect and led to decreases in all injury types.28 Based on our results, a long week of
506	
507	                                                               rest does not have an increased risk of ACL tear compared to a normal week and may instead be
508	
509	                                                               associated with an increased risk of injury. The disparity of findings may be attributed to
510	
511	                                                               differences in injury type studied and number of seasons included in the analysis.
512	                                                                Previous studies have investigated the impact of fatigue on ACL tear risk and report that fatigue
513	
514	                                                               is significantly associated with an increased incidence of ACL tears. 29 Many NFL players have
515	
516	                                                               been outspoken about a dislike for shortened rest weeks.30 During a normal week, days 5 and 6
517	
518	                                                               allow for decreased practice intensity and improved recovery before gameday. Alternatively,
519	
520	                                                               short, or long weeks impede the predictable schedule, potentially depriving players of rest and
521	
522	                                                               recovery days, or throwing off recovery schedules such that player readiness before games is
523	
524	
525	
526	
527	This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
528	                                                               impacted. Soreness and fatigue are difficult variables to account for but could affect the body
529	
530	                                                               mechanics during running and cutting, ultimately increasing the risk of ACL tear. Short weeks in
531	
532	
533	
534	
535	                                                                                                                                                                                   Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
536	                                                               the NFL season may also be used as a mini-bye week. If an NFL game is played on a Thursday
537	
538	                                                               and then the next game is played on the next Sunday, this creates 9-days of time between games.
539	
540	
541	
542	
543	                                                                                                                                                                      Accepted Manuscript
544	                                                               A short week must be followed by a long week of rest in this case. This extra time away from
545	
546	                                                               football activities seems to be preferred by players.31
547	
548	
549	
550	                                                               Increased rest past the normal 7-day NFL playing week may lead to deconditioning. Following
551	
552	                                                               the NFL lockout in 2011, Achilles tendon ruptures were four times higher compared to prior
553	
554	                                                               seasons.32 The 2011 NFL lockout prohibited any organized team activities, leading to a four-
555	
556	                                                               month break from football. Although this deconditioning period was longer, there was a
557	
558	                                                               significant increase in Achilles tendon ruptures. Extended rest and time away from football
559	
560	                                                               during a >7-day NFL playing week may contribute to deconditioning and contribute to an
561	
562	                                                               increased risk of ACL tear.
563	
564	
565	
566	                                                               A limitation of this study is that the data was collected from publicly accessible databases such as
567	
568	                                                               NFL injury reports, so it is possible that all the information is not present. NFL teams are
569	                                                                required to publish weekly injury reports, listing all minor to major injuries. An ACL tear is
570	
571	                                                               usually a season ending injury, so it is expected that the number of unreported injuries are low.
572	
573	                                                               Also, the length of rest in days may not be representative of the rest a player truly receives.
574	
575	                                                               Depending on the team and player, the level of strenuous activity between games could be
576	
577	                                                               different and these stresses could play a major role in frequency of injuries. These limitations are
578	
579	                                                               not expected to affect the primary outcome of this study.

586	                                                               Conclusion
587	
588	
589	
590	
591	                                                                                                                                                                      Accepted Manuscript
592	                                                               From the 2012-2013 to 2022-2023 NFL seasons, 220 ACL tears occurred over 5,694 games. NFL
593	
594	                                                               players experienced significantly higher rates of ACL tears during short (<7 days) and long (>7
595	
596	                                                               days) weeks of rest between games. NFL player position, age, experience, mechanism of injury,
597	
598	                                                               or in season injury timing was not found to be significantly associated with an increased risk for
599	
600	                                                               injury based on short, normal, or long weeks. The NFL should continue to explore the impact
601	
602	                                                               short and long rest times have on player injury risk to determine if changes should be
603	
604	                                                               implemented to prevent these season ending injuries.

                                                               son, postseason, or during week 1 were excluded. Descriptive statistics were calculated to report means, ranges, and percen-
                                                               tages. Data were analyzed to determine statistically significant differences using Fisher’s exact, chi-square, or one-way ANOVA
                                                               tests.

                                                               A total of 524 ACL tears were recorded in NFL players during the study window. 304 ACL tears were excluded and 220 fit inclu-
                                                               sion criteria. 24 ACL tears occurred during short weeks, 68 during long weeks, and 128 during normal weeks. Players were 1.8

                                                               Introduction



                                                               The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) plays a crucial role in knee stabilization and prevents

                                                               excessive motion along the anterior-posterior axis.1 National Football League (NFL) players are

                                                               at risk of ACL tear due to repetitive rapid acceleration and deceleration movements, which

                                                               creates excessive strain on the ACL.2–4 These injuries are devastating, often season-ending

                                                               injuries with an average 10.8 month recovery time, with only 63% of players returning to the

                                                               NFL.5 For those that return, overall performance and production is lower compared to pre-injury,

                                                               with studies showing these players start in significantly fewer games5–7, play in fewer games, and

                                                               have decreased snap counts compared to preinjury performance.8 Of the players that came back

                                                               from ACL reconstruction, only 28.5% were still playing in the NFL 3 years after their injury.8
                                                                NFL players are most at risk for ACL tears if they play the wide receiver position, play on

                                                               artificial turf, or play games during the first half of the NFL season.9–16 Risk factors for injuries to

                                                               NFL players are a growing focus, as rule changes can be implemented to potentially limit injury

                                                               exposure and increase player safety. The NFL competition committee proposes rule changes

                                                               aimed at injury prevention each year,17,18 with previous rule changes aimed at concussion




This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
                                                               prevention and lower extremity injury prevention.19,20 Time between games has been suggested as

                                                               another potential risk factor for injury, with a few studies examining a possible correlation.




                                                                                                                                                                                       Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
                                                               Findings have been mixed, with one study finding no association, and another suggesting

                                                               patients are at a lower injury risk during short weeks (<7 days between games).21,22 Because these




                                                                                                                                                                          Accepted Manuscript
                                                               studies looked only at ACL tears that occurred during 2-4 seasons, additional research is needed

                                                               to definitively determine if there is a correlation between number of rest days between games

                                                               and ACL tears in NFL players.



                                                               To the authors knowledge, there has been no studies analyzing the risk of ACL tears based on

                                                               short (less than 7 days), normal (7 days), or long (more than 7 days) rest during an NFL season.

                                                               Therefore, this study aims to determine the risk of ACL tears based on short, normal, or long

                                                               game weeks. We hypothesized that short and long NFL game weeks will increase the risk of

                                                               ACL tear compared to normal game weeks.



                                                               Methods



                                                               Data Collection
                                                                An online search was conducted to gather a list of NFL players who tore their ACL between the

                                                               2012-2013 season and 2022-2023 season using publicly accessible data. The 2012-2013 NFL

                                                               season was selected due to an NFL lockout prior to the start of the 2011-2012 season, potentially

                                                               affecting injury data. Publicly accessible resources including Pro-Football-Reference.com,

                                                               ESPN.com, NFL game films from 2012-2013 to 2022-2023, and NFL team injury reports were

                                                               Mechanism of injury was determined by watching NFL game film or from a news report

                                                               explicitly stating if the injury occurred due to a contact or non-contact injury mechanism. A

                                                               contact injury was defined as any contact occurring immediately prior to or at the time of ACL

                                                               tear. A non-contact injury was defined as an injury with no contact immediately prior to the ACL

                                                               tear. ACL tears were documented to occur at practice or a game, and timing in season was

                                                               recorded. Only football related injuries were included, and all ACL tears away from football

                                                               related activities were excluded. Playing surface type was determined as grass or artificial turf

                                                               from NFL.com and official NFL team websites at the time of injury. The playing surface was

                                                               identified and recorded for each NFL game from 2012-2013 season to 2022-2023 season.

                                                               Injuries were characterized as short, normal, or long week. A short week injury is an injury that

                                                               occurred in which a player played in an NFL game less than 7 days after their previous NFL

                                                               game. A normal week injury is an injury that occurred in which an NFL played in a game exactly
                                                                7 days prior to their ACL tear. A long week injury is an injury that occurred in a played that

                                                               played in an NFL game more than 7 days after their previous NFL game. Preseason and

                                                               postseason games were not analyzed based on an inconsistency in the number of players in both

                                                               settings and the number of games. Injuries occurring during week 1 were excluded due to

                                                               inconsistent rest periods prior to week 1.

                                                               In total, 524 ACL tears were recorded in NFL players between 2012-2013 to 2022-2023. Four

                                                               the preseason or postseason. These injuries were excluded. (Figure 1) During regular season

                                                               play, 220 NFL players tore their ACL between the 2012-2013 and 2022-2023 NFL seasons. With
                                                                regards to timing, 24 ACL tears occurred during short weeks, 68 during long weeks, and 128

                                                               during normal weeks. During this same period, 5,694 games were played excluding preseason,

                                                               being normal weeks. This was associated with ACL tear rates of 0.037 during normal weeks,

                                                               0.030 during short weeks, and 0.048 during long weeks. Players were 1.8 times more likely to

                                                               Discussion

                                                               The results from this study suggest that players are 1.8 times more likely to tear their ACL during

                                                               a long week compared to a normal week and 1.5 times more likely to tear their ACL during a

                                                               short week compared to a normal week. No other factors, including games occurring before or

                                                               after week 9, player demographics, playing surface type, or years of experience were
                                                                significantly associated with a higher risk of ACL tear during the NFL season. These findings

                                                               highlight the need for the NFL Players Association and the NFL Competition Committee to

                                                               consider the risk versus benefit of short and long breaks between games, as these may place

                                                               players at an increased risk for ACL tear. While short weeks in the NFL season are used to

                                                               increase the number of teams that play primetime games, allowing the NFL to maximize

                                                               advertising revenue, the risk to the players’ health may not be worth the increased revenue. 26

                                                               Previous studies have reported conflicting results on whether the duration of rest between games




                                                                                                                                                                                 Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
                                                               has an impact on the risk of ACL tears.21,22,27,28 Lawrence et al. used different determinates for

                                                               short, normal, and long weeks, (4, 6-8, and 10-15 days respectively) and categorized injuries into




                                                                                                                                                                    Accepted Manuscript
                                                               knee, ankle, hamstring, shoulder, and concussion injuries for the 2012-2013 through 2013-2014

                                                               seasons. Their study reported that across all injury types collected, there was no significant

                                                               change in risk depending on the rest time between games.21 Perez et al. analyzed injuries that

                                                               resulted in a loss of playing time during NFL seasons between 2013 and 2016 and found a

                                                               decreased incidence during long and short weeks compared to normal weeks.22 This study also

                                                               reports a decreased injury risk specifically for linebackers, fullbacks, and tight ends on a short

                                                               week, which was not supported in the current study. Sharma et al. found that long weeks had a

                                                               protective effect and led to decreases in all injury types.28 Based on our results, a long week of

                                                               rest does not have an increased risk of ACL tear compared to a normal week and may instead be

                                                               associated with an increased risk of injury. The disparity of findings may be attributed to

                                                               differences in injury type studied and number of seasons included in the analysis.
                                                                Previous studies have investigated the impact of fatigue on ACL tear risk and report that fatigue

                                                               is significantly associated with an increased incidence of ACL tears. 29 Many NFL players have

                                                               been outspoken about a dislike for shortened rest weeks.30 During a normal week, days 5 and 6

                                                               allow for decreased practice intensity and improved recovery before gameday. Alternatively,

                                                               short, or long weeks impede the predictable schedule, potentially depriving players of rest and

                                                               recovery days, or throwing off recovery schedules such that player readiness before games is

                                                               impacted. Soreness and fatigue are difficult variables to account for but could affect the body

                                                               mechanics during running and cutting, ultimately increasing the risk of ACL tear. Short weeks in




                                                                                                                                                                                   Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
                                                               the NFL season may also be used as a mini-bye week. If an NFL game is played on a Thursday

                                                               and then the next game is played on the next Sunday, this creates 9-days of time between games.




                                                                                                                                                                      Accepted Manuscript
                                                               A short week must be followed by a long week of rest in this case. This extra time away from

                                                               football activities seems to be preferred by players.31



                                                               Increased rest past the normal 7-day NFL playing week may lead to deconditioning. Following

                                                               the NFL lockout in 2011, Achilles tendon ruptures were four times higher compared to prior

                                                               seasons.32 The 2011 NFL lockout prohibited any organized team activities, leading to a four-

                                                               month break from football. Although this deconditioning period was longer, there was a

                                                               significant increase in Achilles tendon ruptures. Extended rest and time away from football

                                                               during a >7-day NFL playing week may contribute to deconditioning and contribute to an

                                                               increased risk of ACL tear.



                                                               A limitation of this study is that the data was collected from publicly accessible databases such as

                                                               NFL injury reports, so it is possible that all the information is not present. NFL teams are
                                                                required to publish weekly injury reports, listing all minor to major injuries. An ACL tear is

                                                               usually a season ending injury, so it is expected that the number of unreported injuries are low.

                                                               Also, the length of rest in days may not be representative of the rest a player truly receives.

                                                               Depending on the team and player, the level of strenuous activity between games could be

                                                               different and these stresses could play a major role in frequency of injuries. These limitations are

                                                               not expected to affect the primary outcome of this study.

                                                               Conclusion




                                                                                                                                                                      Accepted Manuscript
                                                               From the 2012-2013 to 2022-2023 NFL seasons, 220 ACL tears occurred over 5,694 games. NFL

                                                               players experienced significantly higher rates of ACL tears during short (<7 days) and long (>7

                                                               days) weeks of rest between games. NFL player position, age, experience, mechanism of injury,

                                                               or in season injury timing was not found to be significantly associated with an increased risk for

                                                               injury based on short, normal, or long weeks. The NFL should continue to explore the impact

                                                               short and long rest times have on player injury risk to determine if changes should be

                                                               implemented to prevent these season ending injuries.

11	Background: The targeting rule was adopted by the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) in 2008 to discourage
12	dangerous contact during collegiate American football competition. Although targeting rules have been emphasized as a means to
13	reduce concussion rates, there is currently no evidence that targeting plays are higher risk for concussion than other plays in

15	Purpose: To compare the rate of concussion occurring during targeting versus nontargeting plays in American collegiate football.
16	Study Design: Cross-sectional study.
17	Methods: Concussions occurring in games in the 2016-2019 Pac-12 Conference were classified as having occurred during either
18	(1) a play where a targeting penalty was called or (2) all other plays. Targeting plays were further categorized to either those in which
19	the call was upheld or those overturned by the on-field official after replay review. The number of targeting plays and the total
20	number of plays during games were also recorded. Concussion incidence (per 1000 plays) and risk ratios were calculated.
21	Results: Overall, 538 games with 68,670 plays were reviewed, during which 213 concussions occurred (15 during plays where
22	targeting was called and 198 on other plays) and 141 targeting penalties were called. The incidence of concussion was
23	106.4/1000 plays for targeting plays (including 141.2/1000 upheld targeting fouls and 53.6/1000 overturned targeting fouls) and
24	2.9/1000 plays for nontargeting plays. The risk of concussion during targeting plays was 36.9 (95% CI, 22.4-60.7) times greater
25	than that for all other plays. The risk of concussion during targeting plays upheld was 49.0 (95% CI, 28.5-84.2) times greater than
26	that for all other plays.
27	Conclusion: Concussion risk was significantly higher during plays in which targeting was called, especially those in which
28	targeting fouls were upheld.

30	that players should be screened for concussion after targeting plays are called.

Risk of Concussion After a Targeting Foul in
Collegiate American Football
Douglas F. Aukerman,*†‡ MD, MBA, Adam D. Bohr,§ PhD, Sourav K. Poddar,|| MD,
Russell Romano,{ MA, David J. Petron,# MD, Jamshid Ghajar,** MD, Christopher C. Giza,†† MD,
Angela Lumba-Brown,‡‡ MD, Matthew B. McQueen,§ ScD, and Kimberly G. Harmon,§§ MD
Investigation performed at Oregon State University, Corvallis, Oregon, USA

Background: The targeting rule was adopted by the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) in 2008 to discourage
dangerous contact during collegiate American football competition. Although targeting rules have been emphasized as a means to
reduce concussion rates, there is currently no evidence that targeting plays are higher risk for concussion than other plays in
American football.
Purpose: To compare the rate of concussion occurring during targeting versus nontargeting plays in American collegiate football.
Study Design: Cross-sectional study.
Methods: Concussions occurring in games in the 2016-2019 Pac-12 Conference were classified as having occurred during either
(1) a play where a targeting penalty was called or (2) all other plays. Targeting plays were further categorized to either those in which
the call was upheld or those overturned by the on-field official after replay review. The number of targeting plays and the total
number of plays during games were also recorded. Concussion incidence (per 1000 plays) and risk ratios were calculated.
Results: Overall, 538 games with 68,670 plays were reviewed, during which 213 concussions occurred (15 during plays where
targeting was called and 198 on other plays) and 141 targeting penalties were called. The incidence of concussion was
106.4/1000 plays for targeting plays (including 141.2/1000 upheld targeting fouls and 53.6/1000 overturned targeting fouls) and
2.9/1000 plays for nontargeting plays. The risk of concussion during targeting plays was 36.9 (95% CI, 22.4-60.7) times greater
than that for all other plays. The risk of concussion during targeting plays upheld was 49.0 (95% CI, 28.5-84.2) times greater than
that for all other plays.
Conclusion: Concussion risk was significantly higher during plays in which targeting was called, especially those in which
targeting fouls were upheld.
Clinical Relevance: This study supports eliminating or reducing targeting from American football. The results of this study suggest
that players should be screened for concussion after targeting plays are called.
Keywords: head injuries/concussion; targeting; football (American); injury prevention

13	  Objectives:( 1) Evaluate the frequency of same-year, repeat concussions; (2) assess predictors of sustaining a repeat concussion;
14	  and (3) compare outcomes of athletes with repeat concussions with athletes with single concussion. Design: A retrospective,
15	  case–control study. Setting: Regional sports concussion center. Patients: Adolescents sustaining a sport-related concussions
16	  (SRC) from November 2017 to October 2020. Independent Variables: Participants were dichotomized into 2 groups: (1) athletes
17	  with a single concussion; and (2) athletes with repeat concussions. Main Outcome Measures: Between group and within group
18	  analyses were completed to look for differences in demographics, personal and family history, concussion history, and recovery
19	  metrics between the 2 groups. Results: Of 834 athletes with an SRC, 56 (6.7%) sustained a repeat concussion and 778 (93.3%) had
20	  a single concussion. Between group: Personal history of migraines (19.6% vs 9.5%, x2 5 5.795, P 5 0.02), family history of migraines
21	  (37.5% vs 24.5%, x2 5 4.621, P 5 0.03), and family history of psychiatric disorders (25% vs 13.1%, x2 5 6.224, P 5 0.01) were
22	  significant predictors of sustaining a repeat concussion. Within group: Among those with a repeat concussion, initial symptom severity
23	  was greater (Z 5 22.422; P 5 0.02) during the repeat concussion and amnesia was more common (x2 5 4.775, P 5 0.03) after the
24	  initial concussion. Conclusions: In a single-center study of 834 athletes, 6.7% suffered a same-year, repeat concussion. Risk
25	  factors included personal/family migraine history and family psychiatric history. For athletes with repeat concussions, initial symptom
26	  score was higher after the second concussion, yet amnesia was more common after the initial concussion.

Risk of Two Sport-Related Concussions in the Same
Year: Is the Second Concussion Worse?
Kristen Williams, MS, LAT, ATC,*† Tyler Zeoli, MD,*† Jackson H. Allen, BS,‡ Jacob Jo, BA,‡
Aaron M. Yengo-Kahn, MD,*† Douglas P. Terry, PhD,*† and Scott L. Zuckerman, MD, MPH*†


  Abstract
  Objectives:( 1) Evaluate the frequency of same-year, repeat concussions; (2) assess predictors of sustaining a repeat concussion;
  and (3) compare outcomes of athletes with repeat concussions with athletes with single concussion. Design: A retrospective,
  case–control study. Setting: Regional sports concussion center. Patients: Adolescents sustaining a sport-related concussions
  (SRC) from November 2017 to October 2020. Independent Variables: Participants were dichotomized into 2 groups: (1) athletes
  with a single concussion; and (2) athletes with repeat concussions. Main Outcome Measures: Between group and within group
  analyses were completed to look for differences in demographics, personal and family history, concussion history, and recovery
  metrics between the 2 groups. Results: Of 834 athletes with an SRC, 56 (6.7%) sustained a repeat concussion and 778 (93.3%) had
  a single concussion. Between group: Personal history of migraines (19.6% vs 9.5%, x2 5 5.795, P 5 0.02), family history of migraines
  (37.5% vs 24.5%, x2 5 4.621, P 5 0.03), and family history of psychiatric disorders (25% vs 13.1%, x2 5 6.224, P 5 0.01) were
  significant predictors of sustaining a repeat concussion. Within group: Among those with a repeat concussion, initial symptom severity
  was greater (Z 5 22.422; P 5 0.02) during the repeat concussion and amnesia was more common (x2 5 4.775, P 5 0.03) after the
  initial concussion. Conclusions: In a single-center study of 834 athletes, 6.7% suffered a same-year, repeat concussion. Risk
  factors included personal/family migraine history and family psychiatric history. For athletes with repeat concussions, initial symptom
  score was higher after the second concussion, yet amnesia was more common after the initial concussion.
  Key Words: concussions, traumatic brain injury, adolescents, mTBI, sports-related concussion
  (Clin J Sport Med 2024;34:38–43)

Risk of Upper Extremity
Musculoskeletal Injury Within
the First Year After a Concussion
Megan H. Roach,*†‡§ PhD, ATC, Michael J. Aderman,k MS, ATC, Jeremy D. Ross,{ MS, ATC,
Tim F. Kelly,{ MS, ATC, Steven R. Malvasi,k MS, ATC Matthew A. Posner,k MD, COL(Ret),
Steven J. Svoboda,# MD, COL(Ret), Paul F. Pasquina,**†† MD, COL(Ret),
and Kenneth L. Cameron,k†† PhD, MPH, ATC
Investigation performed at Keller Army Community Hospital, West Point, New York, USA

Background: Emerging evidence suggests that athletes and military personnel are at increased risk for lower extremity muscu-
loskeletal injury after a concussion; however, the association between concussion and subsequent upper extremity (UE) mus-
culoskeletal injury is unknown.
Purpose: To prospectively examine the association between concussion and UE musculoskeletal injury risk within the first year
after returning to unrestricted activity.
Study Design: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 3.
Methods: A total of 316 cases of concussion 42% (132/316 women) were observed among 5660 Concussion Assessment,
Research and Education Consortium participants at the United States Military Academy from May 2015 to June 2018. Active injury
surveillance within the cohort was conducted for 12 months after unrestricted return to activity to identify any incident cases of
acute UE musculoskeletal injury. Injury surveillance during the follow-up period was also conducted for nonconcussed controls
who were matched by sex and competitive sport level. Univariate and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models
were used to estimate hazard ratios between concussed cases and nonconcussed controls for time to UE musculoskeletal injury.
Results: During the surveillance period, 19.3% of concussed cases and 9.2% of nonconcussed controls sustained a UE injury. In
the univariate model, concussed cases were 2.25 times (95% CI, 1.45-3.51) more likely to sustain a UE injury during the 12-month
follow-up period when compared with the nonconcussed controls. In the multivariable model, adjusted for history of concussion,
sport level, somatization, and history of UE injury, concussed cases were 1.84 times (95% CI, 1.10-3.07) more likely to sustain a UE
injury during the surveillance period compared with nonconcussed controls. Sport level remained an independent risk factor for UE
musculoskeletal injury; however, concussion history, somatization, and history of UE injury were not independent risk factors.
Conclusion: Concussed cases were more than twice as likely to sustain an acute UE musculoskeletal injury within the first
12 months after unrestricted return to activity when compared with nonconcussed controls. The higher hazard of injury remained in
the concussed group after adjusting for other potential risk factors.
Keywords: athletic injuries; head injury; mild traumatic brain injury; tactical athlete

 "screeningLimitations": "Results come from physically active young cadets, and training exposure was not recorded, so the groups may not have had identical exposure.    "doi": "10.1177/23259671231163570",
   "abstract": "The study examined whether concussion is associated with acute upper-extremity musculoskeletal injury in the 12 months after unrestricted return to activity. Among 316 concussed cadets matched to 316 nonconcussed controls, 19.3% of concussed and 9.2% of control participants sustained an upper-extremity injury. The concussed group had a higher hazard of injury after adjustment (HR 1.84), with varsity sport level also an independent risk factor.",
   "tldr": "Cadets who had a concussion were about twice as likely as matched peers to sustain an upper-extremity musculoskeletal injury in the following year, and the difference held after adjustment (HR 1.84). Staff can watch shoulder, arm and hand injuries after concussion, but the study does not explain why the risk is higher.",
   "methods": "Nested case-control design within the prospective CARE Consortium cohort at the US Military Academy, with 316 concussed cadets matched by sex and sport level to 316 nonconcussed controls. Upper-extremity injuries were tracked for 12 months after unrestricted return to activity, and Cox proportional hazards models were fitted unadjusted and adjusted for sport level, concussion history, BSI-18 somatization and prior upper-extremity injury.",
   "findings": "Upper-extremity injury occurred in 19.3% (61/316) of concussed and 9.2% (29/316) of control participants during follow-up. The unadjusted HR was 2.25 (95% CI, 1.45-3.51) and the adjusted HR was 1.84 (95% CI, 1.10-3.07, P=.019). Varsity sport level was an independent risk factor (adjusted HR 2.53), while concussion history, somatization and prior upper-extremity injury were not significant after adjustment. Shoulder injuries were the most common upper-extremity injury in both groups.",
   "limitations": "Participants were US Military Academy cadets, so the results may not transfer to other athletes or civilians.    "practicalImplications": "Clinicians managing concussed athletes can warn them and their staff that upper-extremity injuries were more common in the year after return to activity, with shoulder injuries the most frequent type.    "rtp": "The study follows athletes after unrestricted return to activity and shows a higher injury risk in the following year, which is relevant to monitoring after return. It does not assess return-to-play criteria, timing or clearance decisions."

  Role of Hip Internal Rotation Range and Foot Progression Angle
      for Preventing Jones Fracture During Crossover Cutting
                Yudai Kikuchi,1,2 Tomoya Takabayashi,1,3 Takanori Kikumoto,1,3 Takahiro Watanabe,1
                           Syunsuke Suzuki,1 Shiori Hiratsuka,1 and Masayoshi Kubo1,3
       1
           Institute for Human Movement and Medical Sciences, Niigata University of Health and Welfare, Niigata, Japan; 2Marutamachi Rehabilitation Clinic,
                               Kyoto, Japan; 3Department of Physical Therapy, Niigata University of Health and Welfare, Niigata, Japan

     Jones fracture is a common injury in soccer players, caused by overload on the ﬁfth metatarsal (M5) that can occur during
     crossover cutting. This study aimed to investigate the effects of the hip internal rotation (HIR) range in passive and dynamic
     conditions and foot progression angle (FPA) on the forces applied to the M5 during crossover cutting. The study included 20 men
     with experience playing soccer. The passive HIR was measured in the prone position. A 3-dimensional motion analysis system,
     force plates, and Footscan were used to measure the angle of the lower limb, including dynamic HIR, FPA, and plantar pressure to
     the M5, during crossover cutting in the 45° direction. Pearson correlation coefﬁcient was measured to examine the relationship
     between variables. Passive and dynamic HIR were not related to the plantar pressure on the M5 (P > .05). However, increased
     FPA in movement direction correlated with a reduction in plantar pressure on the M5 (r = −.56, P < .01). Minimizing the FPA
     with respect to the new direction during crossover cutting reduced plantar pressure on the M5 and thus could prevent Jones
     fracture.

     Keywords: ﬁfth metatarsal, plantar pressure, stress fracture, soccer

1	           sports
2	Review
3	Role of a Ketogenic Diet on Body Composition,
4	Physical Health, Psychosocial Well-Being and Sports
5	Performance in Athletes: A Scoping Review
6	Amy-Lee Bowler 1, *          and Remco Polman 2
7	 1    Faculty of Health Sciences and Medicine, Nutrition & Dietetics, Bond University,
8	      Gold Coast QLD 4226, Australia
9	 2    Faculty of Health, School of Exercise & Nutrition Sciences, Queensland University of Technology,
10	      Brisbane QLD 4059, Australia; remco.polman@qut.edu.au
11	 *    Correspondence: amy-lee.bowler@student.bond.edu.au
12	                                                                                                          
13	 Received: 28 May 2020; Accepted: 21 September 2020; Published: 23 September 2020                        
14	
15	
16	 Abstract: Background: Recently, a focus has been placed on investigating the potential benefits
17	 of adherence to a ketogenic diet in enhancing body composition, physical health, psychological
18	 well-being, and performance of athletes from various sporting disciplines. As the available research
19	 is yet to be collated and analyzed in a single review, this scoping review aims to analyze and draw
20	 conclusions from the available literature that exists on the efficacy of a ketogenic diet among athletic
21	 populations. Methods: Several primary research databases and any relevant citation lists were
22	 searched to locate appropriate studies for inclusion in this scoping review. Studies that investigated
23	 the effects of adherence to a ketogenic diet (KD), defined by a carbohydrate intake of less than 5% of
24	 total energy intake, on body composition, physical health, psychological well-being, and performance
25	 among an athletic population were included in the review. From 814 articles screened, 12 were
26	 identified as meeting the inclusion criteria and were included in the final scoping review. Results:
27	 Adherence to a KD has beneficial effects on body weight and fat mass. Varying effects were identified
28	 on physical health with the diet, eliciting positive effects on fat oxidation but potentially deleterious
29	 effects on stool microbiota and iron metabolism. Conflicting results were reported regarding the effects
30	 of a KD on sporting performance. Benefits were reported regarding athlete well-being following
31	 commencement of a KD, but only after week two. Conclusions: The results of this scoping review
32	 demonstrate that there are both beneficial and detrimental effects associated with adherence to a KD
33	 among athletic populations. It is understood that further research is required to make any concrete
34	 recommendations regarding a KD to athletes.
35	
36	 Keywords: ketogenic; athletes; body composition; physical health; well-being
37	
38	
39	
40	
41	1. Introduction
42	     Over the past 60 years, an emphasis has been placed on the consumption of adequate
43	amounts of carbohydrate pre-exercise/training to ensure adequate muscle glycogen content. It has
44	long been understood that sufficient muscle glycogen stores are required for optimal sporting
45	performance. Advice from major sports nutrition organizations has reflected this ideology, promoting
46	carbohydrate-focused diets for athletes [1].
47	     More recently, an interest in low-carbohydrate alternatives, including the ketogenic diet (KD) has
48	increased. Similar to a low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet, the KD induces an augmentation in free fatty
49	acids circulating within the body. The diet elicits this physiological response by involving a restriction
50	in dietary carbohydrate (<5% of energy intake per day), elevation of fat intake (>60% of dietary
51	
52	
53	Sports 2020, 8, 131; doi:10.3390/sports8100131                                      www.mdpi.com/journal/sports
54	 Sports 2020, 8, 131                                                                                 2 of 16
55	
56	
57	
58	intake), and adequate protein consumption. This restriction in dietary carbohydrate is associated
59	with relative decreases in glucose availability, inducing a physiological metabolic state known as
60	ketosis [2]. Ketosis is characterized by an increase in circulating ketone bodies, namely, acetoacetate
61	(AcAc) and B-hydroxybutyrate (BHB). BHB is acknowledged as the chief ketone body within the
62	peripheral tissues and is the transporter of energy to these tissues [2]. Thus, the elevation of blood BHB
63	levels above 0.5 mmol/L [2] within the body are utilized to demonstrate the presence of nutritional
64	ketosis. During nutritionally induced ketosis, these particular ketone bodies are used as an alternative
65	to glucose and become the main energy source for the brain and other bodily tissues [2].
66	      The KD has gained significant attention due to its potential as a medical intervention for
67	epilepsy [3,4] and its ability to induce weight loss and body composition changes in obese and
68	overweight individuals [5–7]. In more recent times, a KD has generated interest among the sports
69	nutrition community, with evidence suggesting that a reduction in dietary carbohydrate and increases
70	in circulating ketone bodies results in a shift in substrate utilization during submaximal exercise bouts,
71	namely, from glycogen to body fat [8].
72	      A preliminary search of the academic literature did not indicate that a systematic review has taken
73	place to examine whether a KD in athletes’ influences body composition, physical health, psychological
74	well-being, or sports performance. As such, we conducted a scoping review to summarize the current
75	literature to provide an overview of the effects of adherence to a KD. This review sought to determine
76	the effects that occur within athletic populations on both short- and long-term body composition,
77	physical health, psychological well-being, and sports performance in athletes.
78	
79	2. Materials and Methods
80	
81	2.1. Methods
82	    This scoping review has been conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI)
83	methodology for scoping reviews [9,10].
84	
85	2.2. Search Strategy
86	     For the purposes of this scoping review, we accessed a number of primary health research
87	databases (PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, and Cochranes
88	Database) in conjunction with a review of citation indexes and reference lists to locate peer-reviewed
89	studies relevant to the research question.
90	     The search was conducted from inception until June 2020 and considered only English manuscripts.
91	The search terms used to explore the databases were ketogenic, keto, very low carbohydrate, athlete,
92	sport, and exercise.
93	
94	2.3. Inclusion Criteria and Outcome Measures
95	     In order to be deemed appropriate for inclusion in this scoping review, studies must have
96	investigated the effects of a KD, defined by a protocol that involves dietary contribution from
97	carbohydrate of less than 5% of energy intake per day, or blood ketone levels of >0.5 mmol/L BHB [2],
98	and have been implemented longer than or equal to 21 days. Studies were considered if they included
99	male or female participants who were either trained or well-trained in their chosen sport. Reported
100	outcomes may encompass a range of areas including, but not limited to, body composition (i.e., fat mass
101	and lean body mass), physical health (i.e., blood composition, pH, iron status, immune function),
102	psychological well-being (i.e., perceived wellness), and sporting performance (e.g., laboratory- and
103	field-based test performance). In addition, the length of study, outcome measure, and the instrument
104	used to measure the outcomes was reported.
105	     For this review, it is important to clarify how health and well-being were defined when searching
106	the current literature. As this scoping review focused on athletic populations, we decided that
107	various measures of health and well-being specific to athletes would be examined. Body composition,
108	 Sports 2020, 8, 131                                                                                  3 of 16
109	
110	
111	
112	namely, body fat and body weight, were investigated, as this is a particularly important measure of
113	health in athletes that is conducive to their overall performance. Other measures of physical health
114	such as metabolic characteristics (i.e., fat oxidation, circulating metabolites, and muscle glycogen
115	availability), blood profile (i.e., lactate levels, bicarbonate concentrations, iron levels, and blood
116	pH), heart rate, and exercise performance (i.e., maximal exercise capacity and strength) were all
117	considered when searching for appropriate studies. Psychological well-being was identified as
118	pertaining to athletes’ perceptions of the ketogenic diet and their overall thoughts and feelings
119	regarding this dietary intervention and the potential effects on their psychological well-being, training,
120	and exercise performance.
121	
122	2.4. Data Extraction
123	     After applying the inclusion criteria to the studies obtained from each of the relevant databases,
124	we obtained data on study citation details (author, title, journal, and publication year), context of
125	the study (sport involved), participants (age, gender, and sample size), dietary protocol (length and
126	macronutrient distribution), and final outcomes, all of which was entered into an Excel spreadsheet.
127	     Each article was grouped by the outcome measured (body composition, physical health,
128	sports performance, athlete well-being), with three articles measuring more than one outcome.
129	For these articles, each outcome measure was represented separately in the appropriate group.
130	     Due to the nature of the research question, the literature included in the final qualitative evaluation
131	predominantly consisted of studies that employed either a crossover design, non-randomized allocation
132	to a dietary intervention group, or pre–post testing methods. Following selection, each of the articles
133	were critically appraised against the relevant JBI or Centre for Disease-Based Management Critical
134	Appraisal Checklist and were deemed appropriate for inclusion in the final scoping review.
135	
136	3. Results
137	
138	3.1. Search
139	      The search revealed a total of 814 articles related to the search terms, however, only 12 articles
140	met each of the criteria stipulated for article inclusion (see Figure 1). After removing 117 duplicate
141	articles, a further 665 articles were also deemed unsuitable for inclusion, as these involved non-athletic
142	populations, included carbohydrate intakes >5% total energy intake, or involved dietary protocols that
143	were <21 days in duration. The topics that were included in the final review were body composition,
144	physical health, sports performance, and athlete well-being.
145	
146	3.2. Ketogenic Diet
147	     The characteristics of each of the articles included in this scoping review are displayed in Table 1.
148	The total sample was comprised of 101 athletes (84 males, 17 females) from seven sports. The athletes
149	ranged in age from 15 to 41 years.
150	     As detailed in Table 1, each of the relevant studies involved dietary protocols that restricted
151	carbohydrate to less than 5% of energy intake per day. In 10 of the included studies, fat intake was
152	above 75% of total dietary intake. Additionally, in two of the studies, protein intakes were considerably
153	high (40% of total daily energy intake). Of the 12 studies included in the final review, seven investigated
154	the effects of a KD over a three-week period, four ran over a four-week period, and one considered the
155	effects of a KD over a 12-week period.

666	      While the current literature on athletic populations is inconclusive, it is important to acknowledge
667	that several studies conducted on non-athletic individuals have demonstrated that Lean body mass
668	(LBM) tends to be retained following a KD [21–23]. A study on 10 healthy men demonstrated that
669	adherence to a KD over 6 weeks resulted in retention of LBM at week three followed by an increase at
670	week six [23]. This may be due to the energy (29 kcal/kg/day) and protein intakes (2 g/kg/day) that
671	were maintained by participants throughout the duration of this study [23]. On the basis of these
672	findings, it is suggested that future studies on athletic populations concentrate on protein intake or
673	other supplementation (e.g., creatine or leucine) to ensure adequacy for LBM retention and/or increases
674	when commencing a KD.

676	4.2. Ketogenic Diet and Physical Health
677	
678	4.2.1. Acid-Base Status
679	     Acid-base status can have deleterious effects on the body’s buffering mechanisms, resulting in
680	metabolic acidosis. This can cause adverse health effects including kidney stones and be detrimental to
681	athletic performance. In a non-randomized observational study conducted on elite-level race walkers,
682	the researchers found no significant differences in blood pH, bicarbonate concentrations, or lactate
683	levels following adherence to a 21-day KD [13]. This suggests that adherence to a KD does not have
684	any detrimental effects on acid-base status nor does it increase the risk of metabolic acidosis among
685	athletic populations.
686	
687	4.2.2. Bone Health
688	      Optimal bone health is imperative to athletes that are training and competing in high-level sports.
689	Often, athletes competing at elite levels are susceptible to bone injury, partly due to dietary factors
690	such as low energy availability and/or the strenuous nature of the exercise program. A recent study
691	conducted by Heikura et al. [24] investigated the effects of a KD on bone health among a group of
692	elite-level race walkers. After a 3-week intervention period, this study found that athletes had increased
693	markers of bone resorption (+22% CI 9, 35%) and decreased markers of bone formation (−14% CI −19,
694	−9), when compared to baseline values. These results were also observed post-exercise. This suggests
695	that adherence to a KD may have deleterious effects on bone modeling and bone re-modeling markers,
696	both at rest and during high-intensity exercise bouts.
697	
698	4.2.3. Iron Metabolism
699	       When exercise is performed in the presence of limited glycogen stores, certain inflammatory
700	markers such as interleukin-6 (IL-6) are elevated [25]. IL-6 regulates the release of hepcidin, which in
701	turn maintains healthy physiological levels of iron stores. Inflammation increases hepcidin levels,
702	potentially disrupting iron absorption. Each of these responses are likely exhibited post-exercise.
703	Given the associations between limited glycogen stores, IL-6 elevation, hepcidin, and iron stores,
704	it is possible that dietary interventions involving decreased carbohydrate intake may exacerbate the
705	disruptions that occur to iron metabolism post-exercise [25].
706	       A study with competitive race-walking athletes [25] conducted over a 3-week period showed
707	significantly higher post-exercise IL-6 (KD PRE 0.6 ± 0.8 pg/mL, POST 10.8 ± 0.8 pg/mL; CHO PRE
708	0.7 ± 6.6 pg/mL, POST 6.3 ± 0.6 pg/mL) among the KD intervention group compared with those in
709	the carbohydrate-rich dietary group, potentially due to limited muscle glycogen stores. While these
710	findings may suggest that athletes who adhere to a KD may be at risk of iron deficiency, it has
711	been acknowledged that these results are not uncommon following periods of strenuous or specific
712	training regimes. Nonetheless, as iron is a key functional constituent of hemoglobin and myoglobin,
713	it is required for oxygen uptake, transport, and energy production [26]. Iron deficiency may prove

718	detrimental to athletes as it may result in reduced oxygen uptake, transport, and energy production,
719	thus having the potential to impair physical health and performance [27]. However, further research is
720	required to fully understand the associations between a KD and iron status.
721	
722	4.2.4. Fat Oxidation and Metabolism
723	      In a study on CrossFit-trained athletes [28], adherence to a KD displayed varying results regarding
724	fat oxidation rates between male and female athletes. Among males, a KD resulted in an increase in the
725	rate of fat oxidation, however, this was only significant at lower exercise intensities (i.e., 35% VO2 max
726	habitual diet ≈ 0.006 g/min/kg FFM, KD ≈ 0.0095 g/min/kg FFM; 50–65% VO2 max ). In females,
727	the rate of fat oxidation was significantly higher at 80% VO2 max (habitual diet ≈ 0.002 g/min/kg FFM,
728	KD ≈ 0.009 g/min/kg FFM).
729	      Studies conducted on both elite race walkers and runners have demonstrated that adherence
730	to a KD results in increases in fat oxidation rates. Among endurance runners [16], maximal fat
731	oxidation and the relative intensity at which maximal fat oxidation occurs both significantly increased
732	following a KD (PRE 0.57 ± 0.10 g/min vs. POST 1.12 ± 0.10 g/min and PRE 43% ± 5% VO2 max vs.
733	POST 70% ± 4% VO2 max). Similar changes in fat oxidation rates were exhibited among a group of
734	elite race walkers, with peak maximal fat oxidation rates of 1.57 ± 0.32 g/min attained during 2 h of
735	walking at 80% VO2 peak [29].
736	      An increased fat oxidation rate is reflective of increased lipolysis of adipose tissue and increased
737	storage of fatty acids in skeletal muscle tissue in the ketogenic condition. Interestingly, it appears
738	that the differences in fat oxidation rates between genders may be attributed to the higher levels of
739	circulating estrogen among female athletes [30]. It is understood that estrogen affects physiological
740	mechanisms responsible for fatty acid oxidation, however, further research in this area is required to
741	fully understand the mechanisms by which fat oxidation rates differ between genders.
742	
743	4.2.5. Stool Microbiota
744	      Athletes exhibit different gut microbiota profiles to non-athletic individuals [31]. This may be
745	attributed to differences in dietary intakes, including increased protein intake that is common among
746	athletic populations. Murtaza et al. [15] reported that a KD elicited significant decreases in relative
747	concentrations of Faecalibacterium spp. and Bifidobacterium spp., both of which have been reported as
748	being beneficial for maintaining intestinal homeostasis [32]. Faecalibacterium spp. is also known to
749	stimulate anti-inflammatory effects when in abundance. As the diversity of the gut microbiome is
750	associated with several physiological processes that affect the health and well-being of an individual,
751	it is understood that reductions in Faecalibacterium spp. and Bifidobacterium spp. could affect the
752	physical health of an athlete [32,33].
753	      The same study [15] found that consumption of a KD was positively correlated with increases
754	in levels of Dorea spp. and Enterobacteriaceae in elite race walkers. It has been reported that
755	Enterobacteriaceae is often elevated with the prevalence of various disease states within the human
756	body, while raised levels of Dorea spp. have been positively associated with total cholesterol and
757	low-density lipoprotein (LDL) concentrations albeit in hyperlipidaemic rats [34].
758	      The findings outlined in this study indicate that elevated selective pressure on the gut microbiota
759	is observed among individuals who adhere to a KD when compared with those who consume high or
760	periodized carbohydrate diets [15]. Studies have highlighted the potential consequences of alteration to
761	the gut microbiome such as the development of digestive pathologies, metabolic diseases, neurological
762	disorders, cancers, immune conditions, and skin problems [32]. Additionally, this particular study
763	also demonstrated the negative associations between abundances of Dorea spp. and exercise economy.
764	This suggests there are potentially detrimental effects associated with changes in gut microbiota such
765	as decreased athletic performance due to reduced exercise economy and, possibly, reduced overall
766	physical health among elite race walkers. It is important to note, however, that research on the
767	 Sports 2020, 8, 131                                                                                 12 of 16
768	
769	
770	
771	gut microbiome is still emerging and evidence pertaining to the negative effects of a KD on athlete
772	microbiota remains in the preliminary stages.
773	
774	4.2.6. Mucosal Immunity
775	      Salivary immunoglobulin-A (s-IgA) is known to be a marker of the immune system, with decreases
776	in S-IgA reflective of a reduction in immune function and increased risk of upper respiratory illness.
777	In a study on 26 elite race walkers [14], researchers observed that regardless of dietary protocol,
778	s-IgA concentration increased post-exercise. There were no significant differences between diet groups
779	for resting s-IgA concentration, flow rate, or secretion rate. In all groups, there was a moderate to large
780	increase in s-IgA concentration between pre-and post-testing periods (KD 49 ± 45%, high-carbohydrate
781	90 ± 77% and periodized-carbohydrate 77 ± 24%). Moderate increases were also evident in all diet
782	groups for resting secretion rate, but this finding was equivocal. As this particular study involved a
783	period of intensified training, it is understood that the results obtained indicate that increased training
784	load may negate any potential effects that carbohydrate manipulation may have on the mucosal
785	immunity of athletes [14]. In saying this, due to the equivocal results of this study, results should be
786	interpreted with a degree of caution.
787	
788	4.2.7. Oral Microbiome
789	     Among the same group of participants within which stool microbiota was examined, the researchers
790	also analyzed the oral microbiome to determine the effects of a KD [35]. In humans, the oral cavity has
791	been identified as a possible contributor to the onset and progression of certain chronic ailments such as
792	diabetes, cancer, and cardiovascular disease [36]. Currently, studies have also highlighted the potential
793	for changes in the oral microbiome to elicit disruptions to nitric oxide homeostasis, thus possibly
794	resulting in increases in blood pressure [37]. The study conducted by Murtaza and associates [35]
795	showed that KD decreased amounts of Haemophilus, Neisseria, and Prevotella spp. and increased the
796	abundance of Streptococcus spp. Alterations to these particular species of microbiota are thought to
797	reduce the performance benefits often experienced from supplementation of nitrate/beetroot juice.
798	These potentially detrimental effects are thought to be attributed to the impairment of the nitrate–nitrite
799	NO axis that occurs following a KD [38].
800	
801	4.3. Ketogenic Diet and Psychological Well-Being
802	      Only one study in endurance athletes [14] examined how adherence to a KD influenced well-being.
803	This study reported some initial decreases in perceptions of general health and physical readiness and
804	lower mood. However, this only lasted for a few weeks. Following this, athletes reported enhanced
805	well-being, indicating that general health and physical readiness had increased significantly since
806	baseline. There was no clear change in perceived soreness or fatigue from baseline to the end of the
807	trial among participants in the KD group [14]. This suggests that initial adherence to a KD may affect
808	psychological well-being negatively and that it may take several weeks for each athlete to adapt to the
809	diet. After this time, participants report levels of psychological well-being exceeding those prior to
810	the intervention.
811	
812	4.4. Ketogenic Diet and Sporting Performance
813	      The results of a KD and sporting performance appear to be equivocal and influenced by sporting
814	type. In elite gymnasts, strength test results were maintained between baseline and at the end of
815	the ketogenic dietary intervention [12]. This suggests that maximal strength capacity may not be
816	influenced by a KD, however, further research is required in this area.
817	      A study involving eight male endurance athletes demonstrated a detrimental effect on exercise
818	efficiency, particularly at exercise intensities >70% of VO2 max [16]. This decrease in exercise efficiency
819	was indexed by increases in energy expenditure and oxygen uptake that were unable to be explained
820	by shifts in respiratory exchange ratio. In contrast, exercise efficiency was maintained at <60% VO2 max
821	 Sports 2020, 8, 131                                                                                 13 of 16
822	
823	
824	
825	within the KD group. Time-to-exhaustion was similar for the KD group at pre- and post-testing
826	(PRE 239 ± 27 min; POST 219 ± 53 min). Similarly, a study on five cyclists reported no significant
827	difference in time-to-exhaustion (PRE 147 ± 13 min; POST 151 ± 25 min) between baseline testing and
828	4-weeks post-KD [39]. These results may indicate that submaximal exercise capacity is maintained
829	among athletes who adhere to a KD.
830	     Contrastingly, a study that reported on the effects of a KD on taekwondo athletes [11] found that
831	2000 m sprint time decreased significantly among athletes in the KD group (PRE 516.0 ± 37.7 min;
832	POST 484.0 ± 35.6 min). The study also reported significant reductions in anaerobic fatigue assessed
833	via the Wingate test (PRE 55.37 ± 6.16; POST 52.31 ± 7.26).
834	     The study on elite race-walkers [30] observed a significant increase in VO2 peak (PRE 66.3 mL/kg/min
835	90% CI: 63.9, 68.7; POST 71.1 mL/kg/min 90% CI: 69.3, 72.8) following adherence to a KD, whilst at the
836	same time, a decrease in exercise economy during a graded economy test was observed. The latter
837	was indexed by an increase in the O2 demand among the KD intervention group (stage 4 VO2
838	PRE ≈ 60 mL/kg/min; POST ≈ 65 mL/kg/min), suggesting increased metabolic cost and perceived effort.
839	Any reductions in overall exercise efficiency are believed to be attributable to an augmented O2 cost
840	that results from producing energy from fat rather than carbohydrate [40].
841	     While our review provides a brief insight into the effect of a KD on endurance and strength
842	performance in athletes, more comprehensive reviews on this topic are available such as those published
843	by McSwiney et al. [41], Shaw et al. [42], and Burke [43]. These reviews should be consulted for further
844	evidence surrounding sports performance and a KD.
845	
846	5. Limitations
847	     Each of the studies included in this scoping review had small sample sizes (between 5 and
848	37 participants), reducing statistical power. Additionally, the studies that were deemed suitable
849	for this review were of relatively low quality, employing either cross-sectional or non-randomized
850	methodologies. Within the sports nutrition realm, it is recognized that higher quality, larger impact

Physical Health, Psychosocial Well-Being and Sports
Performance in Athletes: A Scoping Review
Amy-Lee Bowler 1, *          and Remco Polman 2
